title: Edward Lloyd's coffee house and the rise of the London marine insurance market, 1689–1774

sources.publisher: University of Illinois Library (digitized text of Charles Wright and C. Ernest Fayle, A History of Lloyd's, London, 1928)
sources.title: A History of Lloyd's: From the Founding of Lloyd's Coffee House to the Present Day (OCR text, Brittle Books collection)
sources.license: Book published 1928 (public domain in the US); facts only
sources.note: 只取事實；這本書依 Lloyd's 的會議紀錄與當時的報紙重建咖啡館的歷史，修正了「Edward Lloyd 創立保險市場」的通俗說法

facts.text: Marine insurance was well established in England by the sixteenth century; it was done by merchants who signed policies from time to time as a side business to their main trade.
Example: in 1559 the London merchant John Gresham took on £25 of the risk on a ship called the Eli.
Around 1700, brokers near the Royal Exchange found people willing to sign policies for a premium that depended on the distance, the dangers of the sea and the risk from enemies.
In late seventeenth-century London, coffee houses served as business centers: people in the same trade gathered there, letters were left at the bar, and newspapers and news were available.
The earliest known mention of Lloyd's coffee house is an advertisement in the London Gazette of February 1689 (1688 by the old calendar) about five stolen watches.
That advertisement asked for information to be sent to Edward Lloyd's coffee house in Tower Street; it does not show when the coffee house first opened.
In 1691 Lloyd moved to a house in Lombard Street, close to the General Post Office and in the center of London's business world.
Ships were often sold at Lloyd's by candle auction: bidding continued until a short piece of candle burned out.
Lloyd printed a single-sheet newspaper, Lloyd's News, three times a week; issue number 8 is dated 17 September 1696.
Edward Lloyd died in February 1713; his son-in-law William Newton took over and kept the valuable name Lloyd's.
No record from Lloyd's lifetime links his coffee house especially with insurance; the historians conclude he had nothing to do with its later role as the center of London insurance.
The Bubble Act of 1720 let the king charter two marine insurance companies, the Royal Exchange Assurance and the London Assurance.
The same act banned all other companies, societies and partnerships from insuring ships, but private persons could still insure ships on their own account.
This ban unexpectedly strengthened private insurers and led insurance business to gather at Lloyd's coffee house in the years after Lloyd's death.
Lloyd's List, a shipping newspaper, began in 1734, most likely because insurers at the coffee house wanted reliable shipping news.
By the 1760s, gambling policies, bets on lives and events written as insurance, had spread at Lloyd's coffee house.
In 1769 dissatisfied serious customers set up a New Lloyd's Coffee House in nearby Pope's Head Alley.
In 1771 supporters of New Lloyd's raised money and elected a committee, and in 1774 New Lloyd's moved into rooms at the Royal Exchange.

notes: 第一則廣告登在 London Gazette 18–21 February 1688/9（舊曆年份 1688，新曆 1689）；通俗說法常寫 1688 年，選文用新曆 1689。
